articles.title: OpenAI Adds WebMCP Site Tools To ChatGPT’s Browser via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.fullContent:
OpenAI is adding WebMCP support to the built-in browser in its ChatGPT desktop app, letting websites expose actions that ChatGPT and Codex can use directly from the page.

This is separate from the server-based Model Context Protocol support ChatGPT has offered since 2025. WebMCP lets the webpage you’re visiting provide tools automatically, without setting up a separate MCP connector.

Site tools assist with tasks like searching documents, editing files, exploring dashboards, comparing travel options, and updating shopping carts. The selection of tools varies depending on the website, so options might differ from page to page.

An arrow appears in the address bar when site tools are available, showing whether a tool can read data or make changes. ChatGPT can automatically find a suitable tool, which remains linked to the page where it was accessed and disappears when you close that page.

Without site tools, ChatGPT uses its standard browser capabilities, such as clicking and typing. WebMCP offers developers an additional choice. It’s different from the server-based Model Context Protocol, or MCP, which links an AI application to a local or remote server and can operate without an open webpage.

WebMCP makes available specific tools from the webpage the agent is visiting. A webpage can register JavaScript functions as tools, including their names, descriptions, and structured input schemas.

OpenAI shared this goal in its challenge announcement:

“Instead of leaving agents to guess their way through your UI, you define exactly how they can use your app.”

Site tools operate within the current page and signed-in session. Developers can connect them to existing application logic and permissions.

OpenAI calls WebMCP an experimental open standard. The specification is a draft from the W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group and isn’t on the W3C Standards Track.

Site tools are accessible within the built-in browser of the ChatGPT desktop app when available for an account. According to OpenAI’s documentation, this feature requires GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra; GPT-5.6 Luna has WebMCP disabled. Site tools aren’t available in Enterprise or Edu workspaces.

Access depends on rollout status and available tools. Although the feature doesn’t work in Chrome via ChatGPT, developers can test WebMCP in Chrome by enabling an experimental flag or joining its origin trial . Some websites might not support site tools, and embedded content may lack these tools. Tools used on one page won’t automatically be available on others.

Site tools can work while you’re signed in and might change website data. OpenAI asks for your permission before ChatGPT interacts with a site and confirms actions like making purchases, deleting data, changing account settings, sending messages, or sharing personal info.

They also warn about risks such as data exfiltration and prompt injection. While each tool invocation receives a safety review, these checks don’t guarantee the website or its responses are trustworthy. Previously, SEJ reported that Chrome’s guidance identifies malicious tool descriptions and contaminated outputs as prompt-injection risks for browser-based agents.

SEJ mentioned back in May that Google’s website guidelines encourage designing sites that are agent-friendly. Now, OpenAI has added WebMCP support to ChatGPT’s desktop browser. This new feature lets website managers choose which actions are available, rather than depending solely on ChatGPT.

While WebMCP gives sites a structured way to expose actions to agents, the documentation doesn’t explain how it might affect rankings, citations, or discoverability.

articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro This is TVNewser’s basic cable network ranker and cable news report for the week of Aug. 17, 2026.

The dog days of summer, which bring a slower news period, are catching up with cable news networks, as all three registered week-to-week declines in both total viewers and the Adults 25-54 demo during primetime and total day.

MS NOW saw the steepest declines in the primetime demo, falling by double digits, while it and CNN also saw double-digit drops in demo viewers during total day.

NETWORKS: According to Nielsen big data + panel for the week of Aug. 17, Fox News averaged 2.009 million total viewers and 178,000 A25-54 viewers during primetime. The network fell by -3% in total viewers and -5% in the demo compared to the week prior ( the week beginning August 10 ).

During total day viewing, Fox News averaged 1.287 million total viewers and 113,000 A25-54 viewers. Based on its average from the previous week’s measurements, the network declined by -3% in total viewers and -6% in the demo.

Fox News continued to rank first in total primetime viewership and finished in third place in demo viewership among all basic cable networks. During total day, it also finished first in total viewers and moved from No. 3 to No. 2 in the total day demo.

MS NOW averaged 851,000 total viewers and 66,000 viewers in the A25-54 demo for the week that just concluded. The network was down -8% in total viewers and -22% in the demo compared with its primetime average the prior week.

During total day, MS NOW averaged 572,000 total viewers and 48,000 demo viewers. It was down -2% in total viewers and -16% in the demo compared to the network’s average the week prior.

Among all basic cable networks, MS NOW was third in total primetime viewers and finished 20th in the demo. It dropped from second to third in total viewers and was 12th in the total day demo.

CNN averaged 584,000 total primetime viewers and 105,000 A25-54 viewers during primetime for the week of Aug. 17. The network fell by -6% in total viewers and -9% in the demo compared to the previous week.

During total day, the network had 405,000 total viewers and 60,000 viewers in the demo. CNN saw its performance decrease by -9% in total viewers and -12% in the demo during this daypart.

Among all cable networks, CNN finished sixth in total viewers and 10th in the demo, tied with HGTV, during primetime. It remained at No. 4 in total day among total viewers and was No. 8 in the demo.

When looking at these networks’ performance during the same period a year ago:

During primetime, Fox News was down -17% in total viewers and -29% in the A25-54 demo. During total day, the network was down -16% in total viewers and -34% in the demo.

MS NOW was up +6% in total viewers but down -15% in the demo. During total day, the network was up +12% in total viewers and +7% in the demo.

In primetime, CNN grew by +32% in total viewers and +42% in the demo. During total day, it rose by +18% in total viewers and +13% in the demo.

PROGRAMMING: Fox News had 14 out of the 15 spots of the most-watched cable news shows of the week, with The Five leading the way with 3.184 million total viewers at 5 p.m. ET. MS NOW was represented in the chart by The Briefing with Jen Psaki , airing weeknights at 9 p.m. ET, with 1.144 million total viewers at No. 14.

The Five was No. 1 in the Adults 25-54 demo, averaging 168,000 viewers. Fox News held 13 of the 15 top spots in the demo, with CNN NewsNight with Abby Phillip , airing five days a week at 10 p.m. ET, finishing with 93,000 viewers to take the No. 10 position, and Anderson Cooper 360, airing weeknights at 8 p.m. ET, with 75,000 demo viewers in 15th place.

articles.title: Zocdoc and Gemini Are Making It Easier to Find Healthcare Providers in Answer Engines
articles.fullContent:
By Andrea Michelson The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

Zocdoc is partnering with Google Gemini to streamline the digital healthcare journey, allowing users to schedule medical appointments without leaving the chatbot. The move comes as an increasing number of consumers search for health information on AI answer engines.Executives at Zocdoc and Google announced the first-of-its-kind collaboration last week.

According to Zocdoc, the partnership is meant to close the gap between searching for health information and booking a doctor’s appointment.

In a survey run by Zocdoc, 85 percent of healthcare providers surveyed said they’ve noticed more patients arriving after having consulted AI to understand their symptoms. The same survey found that 23% of patient respondents would prefer to consult both AI and a clinician in their healthcare journeys.

As AI becomes a starting point for more consumer decisions, appearing in traditional search results is no longer enough. Providers increasingly need to be discoverable, relevant, and ultimately, bookable within the environments where patients are seeking health information.

To integrate the AI-informed patient journey with the online booking experience, Zocdoc and Google teamed up to provide real-time booking availability within the Google Gemini app. Users can simply say or type “Zocdoc” in a prompt to Gemini, and they’ll be prompted to enable Zocdoc access.

As soon as a user turns on Zocdoc access, Gemini will find real-time appointment availability across ZocDoc’s network of over 200,000 providers, Zocdoc founder and CEO Oliver Kharraz, MD, told ADWEEK in an email.

“Users can share the speciality they want to see or the types of issues they need addressed and Zocdoc will surface appointments for them,” Kharraz said. “Patients can just click to book, without having to dial for doctors or search across multiple sites.”

For Zocdoc, the partnership effectively extends its marketplace into a new discovery channel where users are increasingly likely to seek out health-related information. This also benefits providers connected with Zocdoc, so long as they have appointment availability.

When asked how this partnership will surface provider information, in other words, what factors determine which Zocdoc-connected providers show up first or second in a Gemini-generated response, Zocdoc responded that results will be “relevancy-based,” not performance-based.

Relevancy tends to be user-centric, so which providers appear first in Gemini’s suggestions will depend on a user’s location, preference of specialty, availability, and insurance status.

For the marketing teams working to make providers discoverable with AI, a distinction between advertising and visibility has emerged. A provider appearing in Gemini’s recommendation no longer has to buy an ad placement to become visible to patients, but they do need to appear relevant to a given user.

The Zocdoc-Google partnership not only illustrates the emerging distinction between being search-visible versus discoverable with AI, but also demonstrates what it looks like when AI-delivered results are actionable with such an integration.

“Our ambition is that every front door to care in America will be powered by Zocdoc, and every provider will be connected to our network,” Kharraz told ADWEEK. “This is the next step in Zocdoc’s journey as we expand beyond our marketplace, to power access to care everywhere patients search.”

This shift is part of a larger change underway in healthcare marketing. Health-seeking behavior is increasingly fragmented across search engines, insurance directories, marketplaces, and now AI assistants. The brands that benefit may not simply be the ones that show up across various forms of search, but the ones that can turn discovery into action.

Andrea Michelson is the healthcare marketing reporter at ADWEEK. She previously covered the coronavirus pandemic for Business Insider and was part of the New York Times Covid mapping effort in 2020.

articles.fullContent:
By Kendra Barnett ADWEEK House: Advertising HQ brings the people shaping advertising, commerce, and media together for four days of unscripted conversations and after-hours connections. Meet us in Midtown, Oct. 5–8.

A version of this story was originally published in AI, Tech & Money, a free, weekly newsletter packed with news and exclusive analysis on all things tech, platforms, and deals in advertising and media. Sign up for it here .

I’m flying from New York to L.A. today, a commute during which I’ll be listening to Dolly Parton and Dolly Parton only in my headphones. (If you, too, are In Your Feels about the passing of Miss Dolly, make sure to check out our recap of her most fabulous ad appearances over the years .)

In other news, Meta is facing the most material consequences to date over claims that its social platforms put children at risk with addictive features. The tech giant on Wednesday not only agreed to pay up to a record $17.1 billion as part of a settlement with 47 states, but also agreed to limit features like beauty filters and Like counts, and to enforce a new two-hour daily limit for kids using Instagram and Facebook. The changes threaten to impact its core advertising business, as brands will have fewer opportunities to market to minors. No doubt more to come on that.

Speaking of advertising, it’s a big week for one of the industry’s most influential players, The Trade Desk. The company this week bid adieu to its top engineer, Aravind Chandrasekharan , adding to an expanding roster of high-profile exits from the demand-side platform. Also this week, the company is unveiling a reboot of its central ad-buying platform Kokai; the update integrates new agentic features and aims to assuage media buyers’ long-standing complaints about its clunky interface. Paired with a leaked deck obtained by ADWEEK detailing the company’s H2 plans, these may be early signs of a turnaround effort after months of flailing .

Finally, a quick reminder that entries are now open for ADWEEK Tech Challengers to Watch, a new award dedicated to spotlighting up-and-coming tech companies making waves in adland. Learn more and enter here .

As always, replies to this email go straight to my inbox, so please share feedback or tips. Alternatively, reach me securely at kendra.16 on Signal.

Omnicom quietly offloaded hundreds of the engineers and product staff behind its central AI platform to a third-party contractor.

OpenAI is testing exclusion targeting in its nascent ads system.

Streaming now accounts for 48.2% of the total ad-supported TV market , continuing to eat into linear.

Marketplaces like Amazon and Walmart are officially the first place consumers go to shop for new brands, according to recent research from ecommerce fulfillment company Radial . Its research found that 44% of adults in the U.S. usually purchase a new brand via marketplaces, compared to just 21% who transact on the brand’s website and 17% who shop in person.

Deep Learning: Is The Trade Desk’s Turnaround Push Officially Underway?

The Trade Desk, adtech’s Wall Street darling-turned-flounderer, would seem to be gearing up for a concerted rebound effort.

The demand-side platform, which enables advertisers to buy ads programmatically across the open web, is focused on investing in and commercializing new agentic tools, according to a leaked H2 roadmap deck obtained by ADWEEK this week. The company’s big push is centered on a new central AI assistant that advertisers can turn to for help with a range of tasks; the assistant can tap into a suite of specialized Koa agents to aid users in campaign setup, audience building, frequency capping, performance measurement, and more.

That AI assistant is being given a privileged new home within Kokai, the company’s core ad-buying platform. This positioning is part of The Trade Desk’s larger makeover of Kokai, unveiled today in a refresh significant enough that the company felt the need to give it its own branding, Kokai Zuma.

EXCLUSIVE: Leaked Deck Outlines The Trade Desk’s Agentic Plans for H2 2026 As part of the Kokai Zuma refresh, The Trade Desk is also swapping the divisive periodic table-inspired interface for a more standard dashboard design as the platform’s default view, confirming ADWEEK’s previous reporting . It’s a change made in response to advertisers’ negative feedback about the navigability of the interface, leadership has implied.

On the company’s second-quarter earnings call earlier this month, CEO Jeff Green said the company is “listening to our clients and responding with innovative upgrades.”

The changes arrive after an extended downturn for the ad giant. After hitting a staggering $69 billion market cap in late 2024, the company has been knocked down by pricing pressures from rivals Amazon and Yahoo , critical product feedback , rising tensions with supply-side partners , and a public battle with one of its biggest clients, the agency holding company Publicis .

This month, the company posted its weakest quarterly growth since 2020, with revenue up just 3% to $715 million, and its Q3 guidance of $650 million coming in well under analyst expectations of $840 million. Green said the figures were “not a reflection” of the company, while pointing to a bevy of headwinds that included tariffs, inflationary pressures, and weak consumer spending.

Meta grew ads 27% last quarter. Amazon 26%. Google 14.5%.

The Trade Desk grew 3%, and "macro" was the first reason management gave for the miss.

The word came up 14 times on the call. pic.twitter.com/fOXUOAoV3D

— Thomas Chua (@SteadyCompound) August 7, 2026

But Green also used the opportunity to highlight The Trade Desk’s fresh focus on agentic AI. “Agentic is one of the biggest opportunities that advertising will ever see,” he said, adding that in the coming quarters the business will “continue to make our platform easier to use while expanding its capability through agentic workflows.”

He criticized the approach of some competitors to The Trade Desk, who he suggested are slyly repackaging standard programmatic guarantees and fixed price deals with shiny “agentic” wrapping: “They argue that their cheap fee will compensate for their lack of objectivity and their decisions that favor publishers rather than the buyer who is footing the bill.”

The comments fit with Green’s broader criticism of some supply-side platforms’ practices. Earlier this year, he likened some SSPs to house flippers who sell at a markup without necessarily having sellers’ best interests at heart. Tensions between The Trade Desk and some SSPs also flared last year when the company made the unusual decision to relabel all SSPs as “resellers.” Now, Green appears to be taking a twofold dig at some of those players: suggesting they have misaligned incentives when they offer buying tools, while also accusing them of slapping an “agentic” label on basic programmatic offerings.

PubMatic has been aggressively positioning its AgenticOS platform as an alternative for buyers; the system is integrated with its programmatic guaranteed and private market deals. Magnite, meanwhile, now offers a buyer agent and an agentic orchestration layer spanning buy- and sell-side functions. And this spring, Kargo launched Project Kera , an AI-backed planning and buying interface.

As a vote of confidence in The Trade Desk’s potential in advertising’s agentic future, Green bought back some 6 million shares of his company’s stock in March.

The company is also stacking its ranks with a fresh executive cohort that could help it execute a turnaround. In the past three months, the DSP has welcomed Kristi Argyilan, the mastermind behind Target’s Roundel retail media business, as chief commercial officer ; Nate Olmstead, who joins as CFO from AI firm Penguin Solutions; ex-Zendesk exec Sarah Gavin as CMO; and former Google and LinkedIn exec Penry Price as board member .

Paired with a refreshed Kokai platform and a new conversational AI layer, these may well be early indicators of a more concerted rebound effort.

articles.title: Workweek Raises $17 Million, Debuts B2B Newsletter Platform
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Stenberg The business-to-business media company Workweek has raised an additional $17 million to fund the expansion of its newsletter platform, founder and chief executive Adam Ryan tells ADWEEK.

The raise, financed by Next Coast Ventures with participation from Aperiam Ventures, comes two years after the company raised $12.5 million in its Series A in June 2024. In total, Workweek has raised $36.5 million.

The company declined to share its updated valuation. It generates “north of $20 million” in revenue, per Ryan, and is not profitable.

Rather than built around a core editorial staff, Workweek operates as a series of branded franchises, each led by a “practitioner creator,” its term for an industry expert who writes about their work while still maintaining their primary job.

Currently, the Workweek ecosystem consists of five verticals whose content is produced by eight practitioner creators. The verticals include finance, human resources, marketing, commerce, and healthcare, and each has distinct branding—its human resources franchise, for instance, is called I Hate It Here and written by chief people officer Hebba Youssef.

Across these franchises, Workweek has around 150,000 audience members, each of whom has to apply and be vetted to join the community. This filtration process enables Workweek to ensure that, for example, only HR professionals are reading I Hate It Here, creating industry-specific communities that bolster its appeal to endemic advertisers, according to Ryan.

With its new round of funding, Workweek aims to dramatically increase the number of franchises and practitioner creators by making its content-creation tools available to anyone in the network. It already has 35 new newsletters prepared to launch and anticipates that “thousands” more practitioner creators will launch their own email products over the coming year, per Ryan.

“Before we were a content platform, where creators created content and we put it in the platform,” he said. “Now we are a newsletter platform.”

For creators, the appeal of launching on Workweek, compared to rival platforms like Substack or Beehiiv, comes down to the audience.

The natural industry alignment created by the franchise structure means that practitioner creators are creating content specifically for an audience of their own peers. This creates a tighter sense of community than writing for a general audience, as well as drives up the value of its advertising inventory. It also means that new authors have a preexisting community of potential subscribers to tap.

“We’ve been building our ad platform for two and a half years,” said Ryan. “What we’ve done is identify about 81% of subscribers to who they are and the company they work for. For advertisers, we can promise them that every impression is someone in their industry.”

FOR Scoops, Sharp Analysis, and Insider Context

On Workweek, practitioner creators can expect CPMs up to five times the industry average, according to Ryan, with some newsletters netting around $75 per 1,000 readers. Two of its top creators are banking over seven figures in revenue per year, while others can make five figures annually with just one send per week.

Workweek takes a percentage of the revenue it generates across this ad network, although the cut varies, according to Ryan.

Now that any practitioner creator can create their own newsletter, the expansion should grow the volume of content created and shared, both inside and outside the Workweek platform, helping to more quickly scale its audience.

The strategy is a bet on the growing prominence of B2B creators, whose field combines the efficacy of creator marketing with the lucrative returns of B2B advertising. Other companies in the space, including Marketing Brew and Smooth Media, are making similar investments in these so-called knowledge creators.

The strategy is not without its challenges, according to Brian Morrissey, industry analyst and author of The Rebooting.

Primarily, the amount of capital Workweek has raised means it will have to generate a substantial exit to justify its investment, per Morrissey. Following the fundraising excesses of the last decade, in recent years media startups have tried to raise as little funding as possible. The five-year-old company also faces friction in the discovery process, per Morrissey. By dent of its exclusive nature, showcasing content only to approved members of its franchises, Workweek content is not highly visible on purpose. Its decision to operate as a federation of franchises, rather than under the Workweek brand, also complicates that effort.

Enabling more practitioner creators to create and distribute content should mitigate these issues, according to Ryan.

articles.title: i-D Names Michiel Steur as Its First CEO
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Stenberg The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

The trendsetting fashion and culture publisher i-D has appointed Michiel Steur as its first chief executive officer, a newly created role at the 46-year-old editorial brand, according to Steur. He will officially start Oct. 1.

As CEO, Steur will be responsible for growing the brand and its business. He will report to the leadership of its new parent company, Bedford Media, which acquired the title in November 2023 from Vice Media as it navigated bankruptcy proceedings.

The publisher will remain committed to its founding mission, which is to discover and champion new talent, but also aims to evolve from an editorial outlet into a broader media business and cultural platform, according to Steur.

“None of this is about reinventing what i-D stands for,” Steur said. “Our mission is clear, and it’s a priority to execute on that.”

Steur originally joined i-D in October 2024 as its chief commercial officer. His appointment comes at a challenging time for lifestyle media, as disruptions to search and social traffic have upended the open web, throttling advertising revenues while reducing the reach of editorial brands.

i-D will have to navigate those challenges, but the deep pockets of its new ownership group could provide it a degree of insulation.

Bedford Media was founded in conjunction with its acquisition of i-D by supermodel Karlie Kloss, along with her husband, venture capitalist and new co-owner of the Los Angeles Lakers, Josh Kushner. Kloss is also a partial owner of W Magazine and, through Bedford Media, operates Life Magazine through a licensing agreement with People Inc.

i-D has historically been rooted in the worlds of fashion and creativity, identifying and nurturing key talent in the space.

For the first cover story since its acquisition, the company hosted an open casting call and found Enza, an unsigned model from Ohio. Later, she appeared on the cover of the magazine, traveled with the brand to Paris Fashion Week, and was signed to an agency.

Under Steur, the publisher will continue in that tradition, highlighting talent in the arts, including its own editorial staff.

As part of a broader emphasis on treating its staff as creators, the company launched on Substack in 2025, becoming one of the first legacy media brands to do so. Several i-D editors operate their own newsletters on the platform as well.

The outlet also maintains a longstanding YouTube presence, where it publishes full-length videos to its 1.27 million subscribers. Social media and video more broadly are key points of emphasis for the company, which has 2.4 million followers on Instagram alone. Over the past 12 months, its social reach has doubled, according to Steur.

Despite this robust social presence, the editorial brand is keen to lean further in the opposite direction: print.

Its print business is growing and accounts for 20% of total revenue, according to Steur. The company has leaned into the tangible product as a point of differentiation, using the magazine as the centerpiece for larger partnership deals.

It introduced limited-edition print zines built around specific themes or talent, some produced editorially and others in partnership with brands, including a past campaign with Adidas. These sponsored projects include small print runs, often ranging between 500 and 5,000 copies, but the content is amplified on social and digital platforms.

The 30-person company declined to comment on its profitability or overall revenue. Its largest line of business comes from creative partnerships, such as branded content. However, it also brings in revenue from events and creative services, such as doing in-house agency work for brands, according to Steur.

From an advertising perspective, i-D has expanded its presence in beauty, as well as in automotive and technology

As the company continues to evolve, its new ownership will let it invest in its mission over a longer period than a typical media owner might allow, according to Steur.

“The decisions that we make are with the belief that they will grow the brand over time rather than optimizing short-term success,” he said.

articles.title: AI Tools Recommend Brands But Cite Other Sites, Data Shows via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.fullContent:
AI tools often suggest brands without directly linking to their official websites. Shero Commerce’s recent analysis found that only 2.8% of the 1,851 sources cited across Google AI Mode, ChatGPT, and Perplexity were brand-owned pages.

Shero, a Shopify agency specializing in SEO and AI services, looked into citation trends, but the analysis doesn’t show why AI systems favor some sources over others.

Third-Party Sites Received Most Citations

Shero examined purchasing questions across 60 product categories, gathering all sources provided by three different AI tools. Most references pointed to websites outside of brand-owned domains. The biggest source category made up 59% of citations, including sites like Good Housekeeping, Verywell Fit, and Reviewed.com . Brand-owned pages accounted for only 2.8%.

This pattern also appeared when AI tools suggested brands by name. Shero found 159 brand recommendations across all platforms, with the brand’s own page cited in 31% of those cases.. For example, both ChatGPT and Perplexity recommended brands such as Gymshark, Alo, and Beyond Yoga for a squat-proof leggings query, citing third-party sites.

Google AI Mode Rarely Named Sampled Brands

Shero found that in its sample, brands were cited or recommended in 9.5% of relevant Google AI Mode store checks across 60 different categories. In around one-third of these categories, no sampled brands were present.

The report also mentions that popular tools like ChatGPT and Perplexity suggested well-known brands, but Shero didn’t offer a comparable recommendation rate for these platforms. So, while the 9.5% figure from Google is useful independently, it shouldn’t be directly compared to other platforms.

The citation analysis was part of a broader review of product content across Shopify stores. In checking a stratified sample of product descriptions, Shero found 20% were identical to or very similar to those on other websites. These similarities mostly appeared among retailers or marketplaces reselling the same products, rather than between competing Shopify brands.

The authors suggest that syndication could make attribution more difficult when identical text exists across multiple sites. However, the analysis doesn’t show that duplication resulted in third-party sites receiving more citations.

The report also highlighted that short Shopify description fields may underestimate the actual amount of text on a page. Out of 173 stores Shero could cleanly measure using raw HTML, 27 had fewer than 50 words of product-specific content.

Shero collected 8,573 product descriptions from 883 stores with live product data.

For ecommerce brands, being recommended and being cited are two separate outcomes. One brand may be highlighted in an AI buying answer, while another site might receive the source link. Shero’s data offers some insight into the difference, but doesn’t confirm why AI tools select those particular sources.

The main thing to consider is whether changing the product content affects citation behavior. Shero didn’t test if rewriting syndicated descriptions, adding original copy, or adjusting page structure makes it more likely for a brand’s page to be cited. To really understand this, a specific test focusing on those changes would be necessary. For now, the report just shows where citations occurred, without explaining why those sources were selected.

Trellis Prompt:

“Review our publishing data from the last 14 days and summarize the top 3 creative themes that drove the highest engagement. Summarize this for an executive audience.”

The more networks and content types your team manages, the easier it is for conversations and data to become scattered. These updates bring more of that activity into your existing workflows.

NewsWhip, Sprout’s predictive media intelligence product, now folds Bluesky engagement into article-level predictive scoring inside Spike, so rising stories surface sooner.

In Sprout’s Social Listening, the AI Query Builder takes what you want to listen for in plain language and writes the structured query for you, so setup time goes into analysis instead.

articles.title: Anthropic Has Never Signed a Licensing Deal, Yet Never Been Sued. Why?
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Stenberg The future of brands gets decided here. Join the industry’s top marketers at Brandweek for the ideas, insights, and connections shaping what’s next. Get your ticket.

This story was originally published in On Background with Mark Stenberg, a free, weekly newsletter that explores the key themes shaping the media industry. You can sign up for it here .

In response to the disruption posed to the internet by artificial intelligence firms, digital publishers have largely adopted a “ woo and sue ” strategy, striking content licensing deals with amenable parties and taking legal action against the others.

As a result, nearly every major artificial intelligence company, including OpenAI, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, and Perplexity, has signed some form of content licensing agreement with a premium digital publisher, with one notable exception: Anthropic.

And yet, Anthropic is also one of the only major AI firms to have avoided any legal action at the hands of digital publishers.

The New York Times and Ziff Davis have sued OpenAI, News Corp. and CNN have sued Perplexity, Condé Nast has sued Cohere, and Penske Media has sued Google, among dozens of other suits. To be fair, Anthropic has not escaped legal action altogether: In July, it paid $1.5 billion to settle a class action lawsuit brought against it by a group of book authors.

Why the discrepancy? The answer is a combination of fortunate timing and advantageous branding, according to interviews with four digital media executives and an industry legal expert.

“In this interesting space of law and AI companies, this is the most interesting, most important question,” said the chief executive of a premium digital publisher. “The biggest question is who is going to win. But this subsidiary question—why has nobody sued Anthropic—is the key one.”

The query is more than a rhetorical exercise. Anthropic and its archrival OpenAI are both hurtling toward the public markets, with valuations of $965 billion and $852 billion, respectively.

The answer engines the two companies have loosed on the open web have upended a digital marketplace that stood intact for nearly two decades, forcing digital publishers to scramble their commercial and editorial strategies in response.

FOR Scoops, Sharp Analysis, and Insider Context

On Background A direct line to ADWEEK’S senior media reporter, delivering scoops, sharp analysis, and insider context on how publishing, streaming, and advertising are changing.

By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms of Use and Privacy Policy . You may opt-out anytime by clicking ‘unsubscribe’ from the newsletter or from your account.

If Anthropic wins the AI race, its philosophy toward data capture and fair use could become the foundational dynamic of the open web. As such, the company and its relationship with publishers is of paramount importance to the future of digital media.

A spokesperson for Anthropic said the company does have data partnerships, but declined to share further specifics. The company has not announced any deals publicly, and the executives ADWEEK spoke with were unaware of any such deals among their peers.

“Claude is trained on a combination of publicly available data, data we create and data obtained through specific partnerships, based on product needs,” said an Anthropic spokesperson. “Our partnerships team is focused on data partnerships that meaningfully improves our products for our enterprise and developer customers.”

Unlike its peers, Anthropic has not negotiated content licensing agreements with major news publishers for a variety of reasons, according to multiple publishers.

Primarily, the company believes that its scraping and use of publisher content is legally permissible under the concept of fair use, according to all five sources. As such, the company has not moved to enter into any such partnerships, nor has it indicated any plans to do so in the future.

While Anthropic has made its position clear, the firm does maintain an open line of communication with leading publishers in the digital media ecosystem. It named a vice president of product partnerships, Tom Turvey, who joined in February 2024, to manage key relationships.

While conversations with Turvey and his team are typically courteous, the company makes it clear that they are dead ends, according to three of the media executives.

“[Turvey]’s job is to … pick up the phone twice a day and say no,” said the first media executive.

Turvey did not respond to a request for comment.

Additionally, Anthropic executives believe, given the gravity of the technology that they are building, that it is vital that they develop AI before anyone else does, according to the media executive.

In February, for instance, the company revised its Responsible Scaling Policy, an internal framework it developed for building AI safely, to enable it to move more quickly to keep pace with its competitors, according to Time .

“We didn’t really feel, with the rapid advance of AI, that it made sense for us to make unilateral commitments … if competitors are blazing ahead,” its chief science officer, Jared Kaplan, told the outlet.

The decision reflects the importance the company has placed on developing its technology rapidly, revising even its own safety guardrails to prioritize expediency. In doing so, it demonstrates a willingness to reconsider any constraint, such as content licensing, that it believes could interfere with its ability to keep pace with its competitors.

Finally, especially compared to OpenAI, Anthropic functions as more of an enterprise product, catering to the needs of companies and professionals more than consumers. In March, the company was capturing 73% of all spending among companies buying AI tools for the first time, up from around 50% in January, according to Axios .

This positioning informs its data requirements, according to three of the executives, who were told in negotiations that the company has only ever considered paying for unique, hard-to-access data sets, rather than journalism produced by news or mainstream publishers.

“[Anthropic] more or less told me that, unless I had access to half a million medical journal articles in Dutch, that they were not interested,” said a second media executive, who has negotiated with the company on behalf of two separate publishers.

Despite its exceptional refusal to sign licensing deals, Anthropic is nearly alone in avoiding any legal blowback. (Elon Musk’s xAI also has no licensing deals or related legal suits.)

This article breaks down which tasks are best handed off to AI, where human judgment still matters and how automation can give social teams more room to focus on higher-value work.

Social media manager tasks: A daily overview

A social media manager’s day covers a lot more than planning content and hitting publish. Here are some social media tasks that fall under most social media job titles:

  • Analyze metrics to gauge performance
  • Brainstorm content ideas
  • Research trending topics and conversations
  • Manage paid social media campaigns
  • Vet and coordinate with creators and influencers
  • Handle crisis communication, as needed

Which of these are you still doing manually? Look at each task and ask: Could AI handle it? Or does it still need a person’s judgment?

A few years ago, most social media tasks required a person at every step. Now, AI handles a growing share of the daily workload, from scheduling to reporting to the first pass on customer replies.

Here’s where it’s already doing the heavy lifting.

Publishing & scheduling

Getting a post approved and published can often involve a few rounds of email or Slack follow-ups with your manager or other stakeholders. Automated approval workflows remove that back-and-forth by sending content directly to the right person at the right stage.

Choosing when to post has also become more precise. Instead of relying on generic best-practice windows, AI can analyze when your specific audience is most likely to engage. Sprout’s Optimal Send Times with ViralPost uses your audience’s behavior to recommend the best publishing times.

Alt text is another task that can slip when deadlines get tight. AI can help by generating descriptive alt text within the publishing workflow, making accessibility easier to build into the process. Sprout’s Generate ALT Text capability does this directly in the platform.

Reporting & insights

Building a report for leadership can mean pulling data from multiple dashboards, organizing it into a deck and then explaining what changed and why. AI can cut down that work by letting teams query social data in plain language instead of rebuilding the analysis from scratch each time. With Sprout’s Trellis, social teams, leaders and cross-functional partners can ask questions about social performance and get answers without waiting for someone to pull a report.

That also makes social data more accessible and useful outside the social team. If someone in product or customer care wants to know how a launch went or understand customer sentiment, they can get the answer directly by asking an AI agent.

Social listening & media intelligence

Thousands of conversations can unfold around your brand, competitors and industry in a matter of hours. AI helps teams sort through that volume by analyzing conversations for patterns, shifts in sentiment and emerging topics that would be difficult to catch manually.

Within Sprout Listening, Trellis takes that a step further by letting teams ask questions about sentiment, share of voice or emerging themes in plain language and get answers based on their listening data.

AI can also help teams spot reputation risks earlier. NewsWhip by Sprout Social analyzes real-time signals across social and the web to predict which stories are likely to gain traction. Teams get an earlier read on what’s picking up steam and more time to decide how to respond.

It can also draft responses for customer care agents to review and personalize, accelerating personalization while cutting down the time spent writing routine replies from scratch.

AI can pull data, spot patterns and draft a response. But it can’t navigate internal politics, interpret culture, earn trust or persuade a leader to invest more in social.

Automating routine work gives social teams more time for the parts of the job that depend on judgment, context and relationships.

Getting another team to act on social insights takes more than sending them a report. Social leaders need to understand what product, customer care or sales is trying to solve, then connect social data to the decisions already on their plate.

articles.title: The Practical Guide to Google Analytics 4
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Google renamed “Conversions” to “Key Events” in 2024. The terms mean different things in GA4 and Google Ads, so getting the terminology right matters when comparing numbers across platforms. 
  • Every interaction in GA4 is event-based, with parameters providing the context behind what happened.
  • Data-driven attribution is GA4’s default model, using machine learning to spread credit across all the touchpoints that led to a conversion. 
  • BigQuery export is free for standard properties and unlocks analysis that the standard reports can’t handle. 
  • DebugView is the fastest way to catch broken tracking before it becomes weeks of unusable data.

Are you getting the most out of Google Analytics 4 (GA4)?

GA4 has been Google’s standard analytics platform for a few years now. The move from Universal Analytics (UA) was a major shift, but Google has continued updating GA4 itself along the way. One of the biggest changes came in 2024, when Google replaced “Conversions” with “Key Events” in 2024. 

While some marketers might miss UA, there’s no going back.

This GA4 guide skips the history lesson and focuses on what you need to do in GA4 day to day, from proper setup to tracking key events (not conversions) and other impactful metrics.

What Is Google Analytics 4?

Google Analytics 4 is the current version of Google Analytics, and it provides web analytics on a level that allows marketers to effectively analyze important customer usage metrics, not just track traffic.

Before we get into the details, here’s a quick Google Analytics 4 overview. 

Google Analytics 4 tracks the entire customer path across multiple platforms and leverages AI and machine learning to provide more detailed insights into how users interact with your website and app.

GA4 combines cross-channel measurement and AI-driven predictive analytics. It also operates under a privacy-first tracking framework designed for today’s privacy laws, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA). 

These features combine to give marketers a more complete view of how users interact with their digital properties than what UA offered.

How to Set Up Google Analytics 4

Many marketers ask me how to use GA4. Your setup process will depend on whether you’re tracking a website or an app (or both). I’ve broken down each option below.

Google Analytics for Firebase

Firebase is Google’s app development platform that helps you build and deploy apps and games. If you enable Google Analytics when creating a Firebase project, Firebase automatically links your app to a GA4 property.  

If you’re working with an older Firebase project, you may need to link it to a GA4 property or complete Google’s upgrade process.

To upgrade your Firebase account to Google Analytics 4, follow these steps:

  1. Log in to the Firebase console.
  2. Go to Analytics > Dashboard on the left panel.
  3. Follow any prompts to enable or upgrade GA for the project. 

Once linked, you can find app analytics in both the Firebase console and Google Analytics.

Setting up Google Analytics 4 from Scratch

If you’ve never used Google Analytics before or you want to set up a brand-new website, you’ll need to start from scratch:

  • Create an Analytics account if you haven’t already by visiting https://analytics.google.com and opening Admin. Then click Create, and then Account (skip if you already have an account).
  • In the Property column, click Create > Property.
  • Enter a name for your new property, and select a time zone and currency. 
  • Select your industry category and business size.
  • Select your business objectives (e.g., “Get baseline reports,” “Generate leads”).
  • Click Create and accept the Terms of Service.
  • Add a data stream (Web, iOS, or Android) to start collecting data.

Source: https://www.eridesignstudio.com/insights/set-up-a-google-analytics-4-property/

A data stream is a source of information that feeds your GA4 analytics property. It could be your website or your app. Google will guide you through adding each data stream.

Install With Google Tag Manager

For most marketers, Google Tag Manager (GTM) is the recommended installation method. GTM lets you deploy and update the GA4 tag (along with other marketing tags) without touching the site code whenever something changes.

To set up, create a free GTM account and add a container for your site. Google will give you two snippets of code to paste on every page (one in the <head>, one right after the opening <body> tag). 

Once the container is live, create a Google tag inside GTM using your GA4 Measurement ID and set it to fire on all pages. Publish the container to push your changes live.

Verify With DebugView

After setup, use DebugView (found under Admin) to confirm your events are firing correctly. It shows real-time event data from a single device with debug mode enabled, which beats waiting for reports to populate. Skipping this step is a common way for broken tracking to go unnoticed for weeks.

articles.title: The best competitive intelligence software in 2026
articles.fullContent:
If your competitive research involves jumping between LinkedIn, G2, and an overgrown collection of bookmarked pricing pages, there’s a better way.

Competitive intelligence software automates the detective work, surfacing the competitor moves that actually matter. 

Let’s take a closer look at the best platforms for tracking competitors across sales, search, social, and beyond.

Key takeaways

  1. Best tools at a glance: Crayon and Contify for all-in-one platforms, Lumen and Brand24 for social and brand intelligence, Klue and Clozd for sales enablement, and Similarweb and Semrush for digital intelligence.
  2. There’s no one-size-fits-all tool. The right pick depends on whether you’re tracking deals, website traffic, or brand chatter.
  3. Test it inside your real workflow. If a tool requires constant cleanup or five new steps, it’s not worth it.

What is competitive intelligence software?

Competitive intelligence software is a tool that helps companies monitor competitors and turn external information into business insights.

For example, marketing teams might use it to see which keywords a rival is ranking for, while product development teams might use it to catch new features early.

You could do all of this manually, but that means refreshing competitor websites, pricing pages, and review sites on repeat. These tools bring those signals into one place, so you can spend more time deciding your next steps.

Bonus !!!

Get a free, customizable competitive analysis template to easily size up the competition and identify opportunities for your brand to pull ahead.

Download now

What kinds of competitor data does it track?

Most competitive intelligence tools monitor some mix of the following:

  • Pricing changes: A new tier, a sudden discount, or a reshuffled package can tell you a lot about who a competitor is trying to win over.
  • Product launches and messaging shifts: Catch new features, positioning pivots, and changes in how competitors talk about their value.
  • Web traffic and SEO performance: Track which keywords competitors are winning, where their traffic comes from, and which parts of their site are pulling the most weight.
  • Social share of voice and sentiment: Find out who’s dominating the conversation online (and whether that conversation is positive, negative, or somewhere in between).
  • Reviews and community chatter: Buyers are pretty honest on sites like G2 and Reddit. That candor is gold when you’re sizing up the competition.
  • Hiring activity: Job postings can be surprisingly revealing. A sudden hiring spree in AI, enterprise sales, or a new region can hint at what’s coming next.
  • Company news and funding: Leadership changes, acquisitions, earnings transcripts, and funding rounds often signal big moves before they show up in the product.

No single tool tracks all of this equally well, which is why the best pick depends on what your team actually needs to watch. More on that next.

What are the main types of competitive intelligence software?

Competitive intelligence software falls into four main types: all-in-one platforms, sales enablement tools, digital market intelligence tools, and social and brand intelligence tools. Here’s how they compare:

All-in-one competitive intelligence platforms

These platforms try to cover the whole competitive picture. They pull together signals like competitor news and product updates, then package them into competitor profiles, alerts, and digests for your team.

These tools are a good fit when:

  • You want one central home for competitive intel
  • Multiple teams (sales, product, marketing) all need access to the same insights
  • You’d rather get a weekly digest than dig for updates yourself

But, the trade-off: All-in-one tools cover a lot of ground, but specialized tools usually dig deeper in their specific lane.

Sales enablement platforms

Sales enablement tools are built for the moment a competitor comes up in a deal. They arm reps with battlecards, win/loss insights, and objection-handling answers. They typically integrate with CRMs like Salesforce.

Digital market intelligence

These tools track how competitors perform online, which makes them a favorite for marketing and growth teams.

Most cover:

  • Traffic estimates: How much traffic competitors get and which channels drive it
  • SEO and keyword research: What they rank for, where they’re gaining ground, and which gaps might be yours for the taking
  • Paid ads: Where competitors are spending and what their ads look like
  • Referral sources: Which websites, partners, and platforms are sending them visitors, plus the quality of their backlinks.

Social and brand intelligence

These tools handle social media monitoring at scale, tracking how people talk about your competitors (and you) across social media, blogs, forums, and review sites.

These tools typically cover:

  • Share of voice: How much of the online conversation your brand owns
  • Sentiment analysis: Whether that conversation is positive, negative, or somewhere in the middle
  • Trend detection: Topics gaining steam in your market before they peak

  1. Social media monitoring is the practice of tracking brand mentions, keywords, and conversations across social platforms to understand what people are saying about your brand, your competitors, and your industry.

What is social media monitoring?

Social media monitoring is the process of tracking what people are saying about your brand on social media.

This includes both tagged and untagged mentions, whether they show up in comments on your own accounts or in conversations happening elsewhere across the social web.

In practice, that scope is wider than most teams expect. Monitoring covers posts, comments, replies, reviews, video captions, forum threads, and news coverage across networks like Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn, X, Facebook, YouTube, Reddit, and Bluesky, where 84% of U.S. adults use YouTube and 71% use Facebook. Most of those conversations never tag your handle, which is exactly why manual checking falls short.

How does social media monitoring work?

Social media monitoring isn’t just one activity. It’s a mix of signals that, together, tell you what people are saying about your brand, your competitors, and your industry.

Here are the key components that make up social media monitoring:

  • Brand mentions: Track when people talk about your brand across comments, posts, and conversations. This is your baseline signal, and it covers both direct tags and untagged references.
  • Sentiment analysis: Understand how people feel about your brand by looking at whether mentions are positive, negative, or neutral. Tracked over time, sentiment tells you whether perception is improving or slipping.
  • Competitor analysis: Keep tabs on what people are saying about your competitors, including their campaigns, products, and gaps. Their weak spots are often your opportunities.
  • Industry trends: Follow larger conversations in your industry, including trending topics, hashtags, and viral moments, so you can join them while they still matter.
  • Influencer identification: Find people already talking about your brand who could become partners or advocates. Existing fans usually convert into partnerships faster than cold outreach.
  • Share of voice (SOV): Measure how much of the conversation your brand owns compared to competitors. It’s one of the clearest ways to benchmark visibility.
  • Crisis detection: Catch spikes in mentions or shifts in sentiment early, so you can respond before things escalate.
  • Hashtag tracking: Monitor how your branded hashtags, campaign tags, and industry keywords are performing.
  • AI-powered analysis: Use AI to cluster themes, flag anomalies, and summarize what thousands of mentions add up to, instead of reading them one by one.

Together, these signals turn everyday social conversations into actionable insights for your team.

Social media monitoring vs. social listening: what’s the difference?

The short answer: monitoring tracks individual conversations as they happen, and social listening analyzes those conversations in aggregate to find patterns. They’re closely related, but they serve different purposes.

  • Social monitoring is reactive. It focuses on tracking mentions and responding to what’s happening in real time.
  • Social listening is proactive. It starts by analyzing the information from social monitoring to spot larger patterns and trends. In other words, it looks at the bigger picture to improve your social media marketing strategy over time.

For example, social media monitoring identifies comments about your brand online that could use an immediate response from your social or customer service teams.

Source: Warby Parker

Social media listening takes a step back and looks at those same comments over time to see how sentiment is changing.

What is a social media SWOT analysis?

A social media SWOT analysis is a framework marketers use to evaluate their social media performance by looking at four areas: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.

Here are a few scenarios where a social media SWOT analysis could come in handy:

  • Deciding whether to join a new social media platform
  • Rebranding or repositioning
  • Making budget decisions
  • Planning campaigns
  • Identifying emerging trends

In short, a social media SWOT analysis helps you make smarter decisions about where and how to invest on social. It also keeps your strategy grounded in real data, not guesswork.

  • Strengths: What your brand is doing well on social media, like strong engagement, high follower count, or consistent branding. Example: your Instagram Reels consistently outperform your static posts, or your community responds fast to every product drop.
  • Weaknesses: Areas where your brand could improve, from inconsistent posting to off-target messaging. Example: no presence on an emerging platform your audience already uses, or slow response times in your inbox.
  • Opportunities: External factors that give your brand a chance to grow, like emerging trends or new platform features. Example: a rising keyword in your category, or a new video format with an early-adopter boost.
  • Threats: External risks that could hurt your performance, like algorithm changes or increased competition. Example: a rival brand launching on a channel you’ve deprioritized.

Strengths and weaknesses look at internal factors you can control, while opportunities and threats focus on external factors. These things happen outside of your control (but you still need to monitor and respond to them).

How is a social media SWOT different from a traditional SWOT?

A social media SWOT pulls from different data than a traditional business SWOT. Instead of market share, revenue, and supply chain factors, you’re working with platform metrics, social listening signals, and competitive benchmarks that update daily.

Speed is the other difference. Social platforms shift faster than most business environments, so a social media SWOT needs revisiting quarterly rather than once a year.

As the hub of cultural conversations and online activity, social media provides valuable intelligence to inform business strategies. It’s how you discover everything from what trends are taking over to what products people are buying. In fact, the 2026 Social Intelligence Report found that half of one-person teams consider it mission-critical for future growth.

But between crafting content and staying on top of communications, managing social media is hard enough when you’re the only one on the team. This leaves you with little time to focus on social intelligence, let alone extract insights to fuel business growth.

In this post, we provide a guideline on how to streamline social media management for one-person teams. From strategic automation to structured task management, we show you how you can save time and focus on more high-impact work. Let’s get started.

What it means to run social alone

When you’re running social media on your own, you’re juggling multiple roles. You’re the one coming up with content ideas and bringing those ideas to fruition by writing captions and designing graphics. At the same time, you’re in charge of publishing the content, managing comments, responding to DMs and analyzing your data.

You’re essentially doing everything by yourself all at once.

As it is, social media marketers are already at risk of burning out and running out of content ideas. The 2025 Sprout Social Index TM notes that 33% of marketers fear burnout and creative fatigue.

The risk gets significantly bigger for someone who’s constantly overwhelmed because they’re doing it all alone. Yet this is what social media management looks like for most startups and small business operations.

The biggest challenges for a one-person team

To start with, you need to pinpoint what actually makes it challenging to manage social media on your own. That way, you can focus your efforts on tackling those specific challenges. Let’s dig deeper into the biggest problems in social media management for one-person teams.

Constant context-switching across platforms

One minute you’re checking your Facebook stats, the next you’re trying to catch up on all your Instagram DMs and messages. When you’re a one-person social media team, you’re constantly switching between different tasks across platforms. So you’re distracted and unable to focus on a single task, which will affect productivity.

It’s even worse when you’re doing everything manually. According to The Social Media Productivity Report, 63% of social media marketers report not being able to do high-impact work because of manual tasks.

Creative and content fatigue

Social media teams have to always be on top of trending memes and viral topics to keep producing relevant content. According to the 2025 Sprout Social Index TM , 94% of social media practitioners report having to be chronically online to do their jobs.

Ultimately, the social media burnout catches up, especially when you’re the only one coming up with ideas and producing content. That’s why burnout and creative fatigue rank as the fourth greatest fear among social media marketers.

Proving ROI without a dedicated analyst

When you’re the only one on your team, you’re also in charge of collecting performance data and putting together reports. It’s easy enough to point out which content is performing well or how your page has grown over time. But without a dedicated analyst to interpret your data, you’ll have a hard time aligning your social media investment to actual business outcomes.

Keeping up with response-time expectations

Between the content creation and performance analysis, comments and DMs often go unanswered for hours when you’re a one-person team. This could reflect poorly on the customer experience, especially with consumers expecting swift responses on social media.

As the 2025 Sprout Social Index TM found, almost three-quarters of consumers expect brands to respond within 24 hours. They’ll even buy from a competitor next time if the brand doesn’t respond to their customer service questions on social.

3 tips for prioritizing when everything feels urgent

You’re a few days behind on content and your DMs are flooded with messages that you haven’t been able to check. For one-person social teams, it seems like there’s a never-ending to-do list where every item needs to be done “right now.” Here’s how you can streamline your tasks and figure out what to prioritize:

1. Set 2–3 goals tied to business outcomes, not vanity metrics

Impressions are great, but what do they actually mean for your business? Have a clear idea of what you want to get out of social media. This will serve as the foundation for the rest of your social media marketing strategy, shaping everything from your content to your analytics.

Start with 2-3 goals that are related to actual business outcomes. For instance:

  • Growing brand awareness
  • Building a brand community
  • Improving brand sentiment
  • Generating online sales
  • Driving qualified leads
  • Preventing customer churn
  • Speeding up social customer service

2. Use an impact-vs-effort framework to triage daily tasks

Building a framework for prioritizing tasks will help you organize your schedule more strategically. Weigh the expected value of each task against the effort needed to complete it, so you can sort out the order in which to do them.

For example:

Quick wins (high impact, low effort)

  • What they are: Tasks that yield high value and require very little time or money
  • Examples: Repurposing existing content into graphics and bite-sized social posts, sharing user-generated content, customizing social media templates for new ideas, actively replying to recent comments

Big bets (high impact, high effort)

  • What they are: Tasks that yield high value and require heavy planning, time and/or budget
  • Examples: Running an influencer marketing campaign, launching a multi-platform content series

Backups (low impact, low effort)

  • What they are: Minor tasks that don’t add significant value but take very little time to complete
  • Examples: Making small tweaks to your profile, engaging with content from other brands/creators

Time sinkers (low impact, high effort)

  • What they are: Time-consuming tasks that yield little to no return on investment
  • Examples: Manually tracking and analyzing vanity metrics, designing complex custom graphics for platforms that your audience doesn’t use

Key Takeaways

  • Franchise costs range widely. A home-based franchise starts at around $10,000, while a McDonald’s franchise ranges from $1.47 million to $2.73 million per its 2026 FDD. 
  • Every franchisor must provide a Franchise Disclosure Document (FDD). Use it to compare key factors such as fee structures and available support and financing across brands. 
  • Marketing is critical from day one. Brand awareness gets customers searching, but the franchise location with the strongest local marketing presence wins. 
  • Local SEO and geo-targeted paid ads are the two highest-ROI channels for new franchisees, closely followed by social media that stays within brand guidelines. 
  • Franchise earnings vary widely. Franchisees in the food and beverage space can earn anywhere from under $50,000 to over $250,000.

Learning how to start a franchise can be a great way to become a business owner. To launch a business, you need to perform market research, file for a license, create a marketing plan, and build your brand. Buying a franchise location within a corporation that’s already taken all those steps is one way to shorten that learning curve.

Becoming a franchise business owner also enables you to tap into a large brand’s resources and branding, but that doesn’t mean you should leave the marketing completely up to them.

Savvy entrepreneurs who start a franchise business understand the importance of taking all the right steps from start to finish. That’s exactly what I’m here to show you in this guide.

We’ll cover the basics, like how to start a franchise and the initial costs. Then we’ll move on to the engine that makes your franchise a success: learning how to market it once it’s open.

How Does a Franchise Business Work?

In a franchise business, a franchise owner pays a fee to essentially “rent” a brand name. The franchisee runs the business themselves (or hires someone to do so) and must follow the rules and regulations governing brand use.

For example, many McDonald’s restaurants are franchises, meaning an owner (or group of owners, in some cases) pays McDonald’s to use their brand name, menus, logos, and other business assets.

They run their location, pay McDonald’s to use the name, and keep the remaining profits.

A franchise business is a popular business model because it offers owners the best of both worlds: the support of a large brand and the benefits of owning a business.

A few businesses that offer franchising options include:

  • 7-Eleven
  • Taco Bell
  • Great Clips
  • Ace Hardware

Starting a franchise business should not be taken lightly. There are pros and cons to consider before deciding whether to become a franchisee.

Benefits of Starting a Franchise Business

Starting a business gives you more control over your life and income. Unlike starting your own business, however, buying into a franchise offers specific benefits.

More Support

Starting a franchise business is sort of like playing video games on easy mode. The franchisor offers support through training, materials, process flows, and branding to help you get your business off the ground.

For example, starting a taco shop could require months of menu development, taste testing, logo design, and product sourcing. As a Taco Bell franchise owner, however, much of that work is already completed.

Lower Failure Rate

Franchise businesses may offer you a better chance of success than going it alone. When you buy into a franchise, you join a proven business model that works. You also have additional support and business resources that can make a difference in your success.

Built-In Brand Awareness

Building a brand is one of the best things you can do for your business. However, it often takes time and resources.

When you buy into a franchise, the branding is already complete. People already know who your brand is and what it represents. This saves you time and creates a built-in customer base you can tap into.

Better Buying Power

In some cases, you may purchase goods at a lower rate. Many franchisors negotiate contracts with vendors for the entire network, allowing you to spend less on goods and services by purchasing in bulk. However, the flip side of these benefits is that you may not be able to choose your vendors, and costs may be higher.

Drawbacks of Owning a Franchise

While there are many benefits to starting a franchise business, there are some drawbacks to keep in mind. You’ll pay licensing fees to corporations, which can eat into profits. You’ll also have less control over some aspects of your business. For example, if you own a franchise restaurant, you may have little to say on the menu or which vendors you use.

Now that you understand the pros and cons, the next question is: how do you start a franchise business?  This seven-step plan will walk you through everything you need to know.

1. Identify a Business Opportunity

The first step in starting a franchise business is choosing a franchise to invest in. Hundreds of companies offer franchise opportunities: which one is right for you?

  • Do you want an online or in-person business?

Your forecast said this campaign would hit a 4x ROAS by month two. Instead, CPCs are up, CTR is sliding, and leadership is asking questions you don’t have good answers to.

This isn’t a strategy problem. It’s a forecasting problem.

Most paid media forecasts fail not because marketers are bad at math, but because they rely on assumptions that don’t survive contact with real auction behavior. CPC inflation, conversion rate volatility, creative decay, and AI bidding unpredictability all create gaps between what the model projected and what the campaign actually delivered.

This post covers what causes those gaps and how to build paid media forecasting models that account for real-world variables from the start, so your next forecast holds up.

Why Paid Media Forecasts Miss

Most paid forecasts break at the same pressure points. Identifying which variable caused a miss is as important as building the next forecast, because the same failure tends to repeat if you don’t isolate the cause.

Source

CPC inflation. CPCs are driven by auction dynamics, not advertiser intention. Competitive pressure, quality score changes, and platform algorithm updates can push CPCs above forecast assumptions faster than most models account for. NP Digital data from campaigns across industries shows CPC inflation leads paid forecast failures at 54 percent, making it the single most common cause of forecast drift.

Conversion rate volatility. Conversion rates don’t hold steady across changing conditions. They compress when buyer confidence drops and expand during periods of strong demand, regardless of traffic quality. A constant conversion rate assumption during an economic downturn is actually a win. A constant assumption during a category boom is a miss waiting to happen. Volatility in conversion rates is always relative to what’s happening outside the platform.

Creative decay. As creative fatigue sets in across any audience, CTR drops and effective CPCs rise. If the forecast doesn’t account for a creative refresh cadence, the model drifts optimistic over the life of the campaign. Creative decay is not an edge case. It is a predictable curve.

AI bidding unpredictability. Automated bidding systems on Google Ads and Meta optimize toward signals the advertiser does not fully control. Teams often assume they can compensate for a weak period by adjusting bids. In practice, bid strategy changes have less direct impact than most assume, because the algorithm is making more of the decisions.

Audience overlap across platforms. When the same audience is targeted across multiple channels simultaneously, reach projections overstate real incremental reach and efficiency metrics overstate actual performance. A lead attributed to paid search and a lead attributed to paid social may be the same person, and the forecast rarely accounts for that.

The Ramp-Up Curve: Why New Campaigns Run Negative First

Forecasting average performance from day one is one of the most reliable ways to lose leadership trust in a new campaign. New paid campaigns almost always run negative through the first several weeks, and a forecast that doesn’t show this sets expectations the campaign will fail to meet before it finds its footing.

The reason is structural. New campaigns require time for bid algorithms to gather enough conversion signals to optimize effectively, for audience targeting to sharpen based on early engagement data, and for creative performance data to inform delivery decisions. During this learning phase, CPCs are typically higher than steady state and conversion rates are lower. That combination produces a negative return that looks like failure but is actually normal.

This effect is most pronounced in Performance Max and Advantage+ campaigns, where the algorithm has broader targeting latitude and less historical data to draw on at launch. Campaigns built on new creative, new landing pages, or new audiences extend the ramp-up period further.

The practical implication for ad forecasting is to model week-by-week profitability, not campaign-average profitability. A campaign that looks marginally profitable in aggregate may be deeply negative in weeks one through three and significantly profitable from week six onward. A flat average across the campaign period hides the early risk and the later opportunity, and gives leadership no framework for interpreting early results.

Teams that show leadership the ramp-up curve before it happens get the time to let campaigns mature. Teams that don’t tend to get pulled before the algorithm has learned anything useful.

A reliable forecast marketing campaign model answers questions in sequence: how many people will see your ads, how many will act on them, and what will the business get in return. Key takeaways

  1. The 10 types of social media interactions are comments, shares, saves, direct messages, tags and mentions, likes and reactions, follows and unfollows, reviews and ratings, social search actions, and interactive content like polls and quizzes.
  2. Not all interactions carry equal weight. Comments, shares, saves, and DMs signal stronger intent than likes alone and have a bigger impact on reach and conversions.
  3. Measuring interaction quality, not just volume, helps teams prove social’s business impact and refine their strategy.
  4. A connected social operating system like Hootsuite Social OS helps teams track, respond to, and learn from interactions across every platform in one place.

What is social media interaction?

Social media interaction is any exchange between a brand and a user on a social platform. That includes likes, comments, direct messages, tags, saves, shares, reviews, and follows.

Interactions happen everywhere 5.75 billion people spend time on social, not just in the feed. They show up in stories, in comment threads, in the DM inbox, and increasingly in search results inside apps like TikTok and Instagram.

The key thing to remember is that interaction is two-way communication. A user can start it, or your brand can. Both directions count, and both shape how people see you.
